title: The charge that Christians shun the educated
source_text: Εἶθ᾿ ἑξῆς τούτοις ὁ Κέλσος τὰ ὑπὸ ὀλίγων πάνυ παρὰ τὴν διδασκαλίαν Ἰησοῦ λεγόμενα νομιζομένων Χριστιανῶν. οὐ φρονιμωτέρων. ὡς οἴεται, ἀλλ᾿ ἀμαθεστάτων, φέρων φησὶ τοιαῦτα ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν προστάσσεσθαι· μηδεὶς προσίτω πεπαιδευμένος. μηδεὶς σοφὸς, μηδεὶς φρόνιμος· κακὰ γὰρ ταῦτα νομίζεται παρ᾿ ἡμῖν· ἀλλ᾿ εἴ τις ἀμαθὴς, εἴ τις ἀνόητος, εἴ τις ἀπαίδευτος, εἴ τις νήπιος, θαῤῥῶν ἡκέτω. τούτους γὰρ ἀξίους (εἶναι) τοῦ σφετέρου θεοῦ αὐτόθεν ὁμολογοῦντες, δῆλοί εἰσιν ὅτι μόνους τοὺς ἠλιθίους καὶ ἀγεννεῖς καὶ ἀναισθήτους καὶ ἀνδράποδα καὶ γύναια καὶ παιδάρια πείθειν ἐθέλουσί τε καὶ δύνανται. καὶ πρὸς ταῦτα δέ φαμεν ὅτι. ὥσπερ εἴ τις. τοῦ Ἰησοῦ διδάσκοντος τὰ περὶ σωφροσύνης καὶ λέγοντος· „ὃς ἐὰν ἐμβλέψῃ γυναικὶ πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι. ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ“, ἑώρα (τινὰς) ὀλίγους ἀπὸ τῶν τοσούτων Χριστιανοὺς εἶναι νομιζομένους ἀκολάστως ζῶντας, εὐλογώτατα μὲν (ἂν) αὐτοῖς ἐνεκάλει παρὰ τὴν Ἰησοῦ βιοῦσι διδασκαλίαν ἀλογώτατα δ᾿ ἂν ἐποίησεν, εἰ τὸ κατ᾿ ἐκείνων ἔγκλημα τῷ λόγῳ προσῆπτεν· οὕτως ἐὰν εὑρίσκηται οὐδενὸς ἧττον ὁ Χριστιανῶν λόγος ἐπὶ σοφίαν προκαλούμενος, ἐγκλητέον μὲν ἔσται τοῖς συναγορεύουσι τῇ σφῶν ἀμαθίᾳ καὶ λέγουσιν οὐ ταῦτα μὲν, ἅπερ ὁ Κέλσος ἀνέγραψεν (οὐδὲ γὰρ οὕτως ἀναισχύντως. κἂν ἰδιῶταί τινες ὦσι καὶ ἀμαθεῖς, λέγουσιν), ἕτερα δὲ πολλῷ ἐλάττονα καὶ ἀποτρεπτικὰ τοῦ ἀσκεῖν σοφίαν.
pass_a_gloss: Then next to these Celsus, bringing (φέρω) the things said by very few contrary to (παρά) the teaching (διδασκαλία) of Jesus, of [people] reckoned (νομίζω) Christians, not more prudent, as he thinks, but most unlearned, says such things are commanded (προστάσσω) by them: ‘Let no one approach (πρόσειμι) [who is] educated, no one wise (σοφός), no one prudent (φρόνιμος); for these are thought evil (κακά) among us; but if anyone [is] unlearned (ἀμαθής), if anyone senseless (ἀνόητος), if anyone uneducated (ἀπαίδευτος), if anyone an infant (νήπιος), taking courage (θαρρέω) let him come. For agreeing (ὁμολογέω) straightway (αὐτόθεν) that these are worthy (ἄξιος) of their own (σφέτερος) God, they are clear (δῆλοι) that only the silly (ἠλίθιοι) and ignoble (ἀγεννεῖς) and senseless (ἀναίσθητοι) and slaves (ἀνδράποδα) and little women (γύναια) and little children (παιδάρια) they both wish (ἐθέλω) and are able (δύναμαι) to persuade (πείθω).’ And toward these we say that, just as if someone, Jesus teaching the [things] about self-control (σωφροσύνη) and saying ‘whoever looks at (ἐμβλέπω) a woman toward desiring (ἐπιθυμέω), already committed adultery (μοιχεύω) with her in his heart (καρδία),’ saw some few from so many reckoned to be Christians living licentiously (ἀκολάστως), most reasonably (εὐλογώτατα) would he charge (ἐγκαλέω) them as living contrary to the teaching of Jesus, but most unreasonably (ἀλογώτατα) would he act, if he attached (προσάπτω) the charge (ἔγκλημα) against those to the teaching (λόγος); so, if the word of Christians is found calling forth (προκαλέομαι) to wisdom (σοφία) no less than any, [blame] will have to be charged (ἐγκλητέον) to those who speak in support of (συναγορεύω) their own ignorance (ἀμαθία) and say not these things which Celsus recorded (ἀναγράφω) (for not so shamelessly (ἀναισχύντως), even if some are laymen (ἰδιῶται) and unlearned, do they speak), but other things much lesser and turning away (ἀποτρεπτικά) from practising (ἀσκέω) wisdom.
pass_b_english: Next after this Celsus brings forward what is said, contrary to the teaching of Jesus, by a very few who are thought to be Christians, not, as he supposes, the more intelligent, but the most ignorant; and he says that they give orders such as these: “ ‘Let no one who is educated come near, no one wise, no one sensible; for these things are counted evil among us. But if anyone is ignorant, if anyone is foolish, if anyone is uneducated, if anyone is a child, let him come with confidence.’ For by admitting outright that these are worthy of their God, they make it plain that they wish to persuade, and are able to persuade, only the simple-minded, the low-born and the dull, slaves, silly women and little children.”

To this too we reply as follows. Suppose that, while Jesus teaches about self-control and says, “Whoever looks at a woman so as to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28), someone saw a few, out of so many who are thought to be Christians, living licentiously. He would be entirely reasonable in blaming them for living contrary to the teaching of Jesus, but he would act entirely unreasonably if he fastened the charge against them on the teaching itself. In the same way, if the teaching of Christians is found to summon people to wisdom as much as any other, then the blame must fall on those who plead in defence of their own ignorance, and who say, not the things Celsus recorded (for even if some are unlettered and ignorant, they do not speak so shamelessly), but other things, far milder, that turn people away from the pursuit of wisdom.

choices.choice: The sentence beginning τούτους γὰρ ἀξίους … δύνανται is taken as the continuation of Celsus's words (it describes Christians in the third person, as Celsus does), so it stays inside his quotation; the supplied (εἶναι) is translated. ‘their God’ (τοῦ σφετέρου θεοῦ) is capitalised because Celsus means the God of the Christians. Matthew 5:28 is quoted loosely (ὃς ἐὰν ἐμβλέψῃ γυναικὶ for the Gospel's πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα); the English follows Origen's wording. The editorial supplements (τινὰς) and (ἂν) are translated. ὁ λόγος here and ὁ Χριστιανῶν λόγος are rendered ‘the teaching’, not ‘the Word’, since Origen means the Christian message. The final sentence has ἐγκλητέον μὲν with no answering δέ; the implied contrast (blame the people, not the teaching) is carried by ‘then the blame must fall on’, with nothing added. πολλῷ ἐλάττονα (‘much lesser’) rendered ‘far milder’, since Origen means less extreme than what Celsus reports. Reviewer: the injunction Celsus puts in Christian mouths (‘Let no one … with confidence’) is set in single quotes inside Celsus's double quotes, so his own comment that follows (τούτους γὰρ …) stays visibly his.
Nested the Christian injunction Celsus reports in single quotes inside his double-quoted words, separating it from Celsus's own comment
Removed added ‘still’ in ‘far milder, that turn people away’ (Greek has plain καί)
Checked Matthew 5:28 against Origen's loose wording; no other change
